t.3.27.1: Seeing Dūṣaṇa slain in battle together with Triśiras, and seeing the valour of Rāma, even Khara was seized with fear.
t.3.27.2: He saw the mighty and irresistible rākṣasa army slain by Rāma alone, and Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras slain as well.
t.3.27.3: Seeing that army of his almost entirely slain, the rākṣasa Khara, dejected in mind, advanced upon Rāma, as Namuci once advanced upon Vāsava.
t.3.27.4: Drawing his mighty bow, Khara hurled at Rāma iron arrows that feed on blood, like enraged venomous serpents.
t.3.27.5: Twanging his bowstring again and again and displaying his weapons with practised skill, Khara, mounted on his chariot, ranged with his arrows along the many courses of the battle.
t.3.27.6: That great chariot-warrior filled all the directions and the intermediate directions with arrows; seeing him, Rāma too drew his very mighty bow to the full.
t.3.27.7: With his unbearable arrows, like fires with sparks, he left no gap in the sky, as the rain-god Parjanya does with his showers.
t.3.27.8: With the sharp arrows loosed by Khara and Rāma, the sky all around became no sky at all, crowded with shafts on every side.
t.3.27.9: As the two fought fiercely with each other, each furious in his eagerness to slay the other, the sun, veiled by a net of arrows, no longer shone.
t.3.27.10: Then in battle he struck Rāma with nālīka and nārāca arrows and with sharp-pointed vikarṇi arrows, as one strikes a mighty elephant with goads.
t.3.27.11: All beings beheld that rākṣasa standing firm upon his chariot, bow in hand, like Antaka, Death himself, with the noose in his hand.
t.3.27.12: Seeing him, valiant like a lion and moving with a lion's bold stride, Rāma was not alarmed, just as a lion is not alarmed by some lesser beast.
t.3.27.13: Then Khara, in his great chariot shining like the sun, rushed upon Rāma in battle, like a moth flying into a fire.
t.3.27.14: Then Khara, displaying the swiftness of his hand, cut through the bow of the great-souled Rāma, together with its arrow, at the place of the grip.
t.3.27.15: Then he, enraged, took up seven more arrows, which shone like the thunderbolt of Śakra, and struck him on his armour in the battle.
t.3.27.16: Then, struck by the well-jointed arrows loosed by Khara, the armour of Rāma, who shone with the splendour of the sun, fell to the ground.
t.3.27.17: Pierced with arrows in all his limbs, that Rāghava, Rāma, enraged, shone forth on the battlefield like a smokeless fire blazing.
t.3.27.18: Then Rāma, the destroyer of foes, to bring about his enemy's end, strung another great bow with a deep, resounding twang.
t.3.27.19: Raising that excellent bow, the very mighty bow of Viṣṇu that had been bestowed upon him by the great sage, he rushed at Khara.
t.3.27.20: Then Rāma, greatly enraged, with arrows having golden feathered shafts and smooth, well-bent joints, cut down the banner of Khara in the battle.
t.3.27.21: That beautiful golden banner, cut into many pieces, fell to the earth like the sun descending at the command of the gods.
t.3.27.22: Enraged, Khara, who knew the vital points, pierced that Rāma in his limbs and in the heart with four arrows, as one pierces an elephant with lances.
t.3.27.23: That Rāma, pierced by many arrows released from Khara's bow, his limbs drenched with blood, became exceedingly enraged.
t.3.27.24: He, the foremost of bowmen, a supreme archer, grasped his bow in that great battle and released six well-aimed arrows.
t.3.27.25: He planted one arrow in his head and then two in his arms, and with three crescent-headed arrows he struck him in the chest.
t.3.27.26: Then afterwards the one of great splendor, enraged and eager to slay the rākṣasa, took up thirteen iron arrows, radiant like the sun and whetted on stone.
t.3.27.27: Then in battle he cut through his yoke with one arrow, the four horses with four, and with the sixth the head of Khara's charioteer.
t.3.27.28: With three arrows the strong one cut the chariot's triple bamboo frame, and with two the mighty one cut its axle; with the twelfth arrow he cut Khara's bow along with its arrow. Then Rāghava, equal to Indra, as if laughing, pierced Khara in battle with a thirteenth arrow that was like a thunderbolt.
t.3.27.29: Then Khara, his bow shattered, his chariot lost, his horses slain and his charioteer killed, leapt down with a mace in his hand and stood upon the ground.
t.3.27.30: Then the gods and the great sages, having come together and assembled, standing upon the tops of their celestial chariots, joyful and with joined palms, honoured that deed of Rāma, the great chariot-warrior.
